headline: Pinned: Ukraine carried out a large-scale, combined missile strike on Donetsk today, using a mix of FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles, Storm Shadow/SCALP-EG cruise missiles, and potentially another unidentified munition. Two separate targets were struck. Six missiles hit an underground parking facility at an unfinished residential complex, while another seven struck an industrial building. Ukrainian channels claim both locations were being used to store large quantities of military equipment, including missile and rocket launchers, armored vehicles, and personnel. Several fragments with folded wings, typically associated with glide bombs and jet-powered stand-off munitions, were recovered. Based on the surviving markings, at least some of the munitions used in the strike have been identified as Storm Shadow/SCALP-EG cruise missiles. One fragment bears a manufacturer’s plate marked MBDA FRANCE, along with the manufacturer code F0555. Another fragment contains a toothed mechanism, serial number 10625, and the date 20.08.2024. This is likely part of the mechanism used to deploy or control the missile’s wing. As for the unidentified munition, one possibility is a weapon developed under the U.S. Extended-Range Attack Missile (ERAM) program. However, no confirmed photographs of an intact ERAM missile have emerged so far, making this identification highly speculative. Another possibility is the AGM-158A JASSM air-launched cruise missile.

headline: I've said this months ago, and I'll say it again: based on what I've been hearing from Russian military circles, a new offensive from the north is likely to begin in the winter. There are two possible scenarios. The first, and less likely, is that the Russian Armed Forces launch a new offensive from Bryansk Oblast into Chernihiv Oblast, while simultaneously opening new axes of advance in Kharkiv and Sumy Oblasts. The second, and more likely scenario, is a joint Russian-Belarusian offensive from the north, alongside offensives from the other locations I mentioned previously. This is also what I've been told by several Russians familiar with the situation. Why do I consider the second scenario more plausible? Lukashenko has made repeated, unannounced trips to Moscow for high-level meetings with Vladimir Putin, with the public apparently unaware that these visits were even taking place. Now, Lukashenko has ordered a rapid combat-readiness inspection. You can find more details about that in the quoted post. I'm not presenting any of this as fact, nor am I claiming that the information I've received is 100% accurate. I'm simply saying that this is where the current indicators appear to be pointing. Another interesting development is CIA Director John Ratcliffe's visit to Moscow two days ago. He reportedly offered to de-escalate the conflict. One particularly interesting claim, although I'm not entirely certain about it, is that he proposed a ceasefire specifically in Sumy and Kharkiv Oblasts. That is unusual because there is currently no major ground fighting in either oblast, only sporadic shelling, along with ongoing drone and missile strikes. If accurate, this could suggest that the CIA has some insight into Moscow's intentions to launch new offensives in these areas.

The shift comes after U.S. backed negotiations failed to produce an agreement. Moscow continues to demand Ukrainian concessions, including territory in Donetsk, while Kyiv has rejected those terms. Expectations for upcoming U.S.- Russian diplomatic contacts are reportedly low. The escalation is occurring amid an expanding exchange of strikes. Ukraine has targeted Russian oil and logistics infrastructure, while Russia has continued attacks on Ukrainian energy and other infrastructure. headline: Overnight, a major flash flood struck the Nepal–Tibet border region, killing at least nine people and leaving hundreds missing. Video compiled by the BBC show the waters rapidly rising across the region. The flooding hit communities along the Lhende Khola River, sweeping away roads, bridges, homes and hydropower infrastructure. A massive mudslide also struck Gyirong Port, a major crossing between Nepal and Tibet, cutting roads, communications and power connections. Local authorities suspect an earthquake triggered an ice and rock avalanche into the river, producing the sudden surge of water. The scale of the incident is still unfolding. At least 348 people have been reported missing, including 105 Indians, 93 Nepalis, three Americans and 12 British nationals. Eight South Koreans working at a hydropower project are also missing. Authorities are warning that the danger may not be over. A blockage remains upstream on the Lhende Khola, raising the possibility of another major flood. Nepali and Chinese authorities are conducting rescue operations, with 574 Chinese rescuers deployed to the affected border crossing. India and South Korea are also coordinating assistance. Rescue helicopters have so far been unable to land in some areas because of the flooding and debris.
